title: Burst capacity failure — hypothesis & signal playbook
content:
Purpose:
This doc is a working playbook and hypothesis log for a recurring production class: 'burst capacity failure' in Dedicated GPU pools. We observed intermittent multi-node tail-latency spikes and degraded throughput during customer burst windows. The goal here is twofold: (1) capture runbook steps that helped restore steady-state quickly, and (2) record hypotheses and signal definitions for faster triage on future occurrences.

Executive summary (tl;dr):
- Symptom: sudden p99/p999 generation latency spikes across a subset of a dedicated GPU pool; total token throughput drops despite headroom on some nodes.
- Immediate mitigations that restored traffic: isolate noisy tenants (migrate pods off offending nodes), enable temporary model-variant fallback to lower-memory quantized variant, force KV-cache warmup on newly scheduled nodes.
- Root causes under consideration (not confirmed): noisy affinity/pack scheduling producing cache fragmentation, autoscaler cooldown miscalculation that overprovisioned small slices then evicted too aggressively, small percentage of nodes exhibiting driver/firmware-induced thermal throttling under burst loads.

Observed signals and correlated metrics (what to look at):
- Latency signals: generation_p99_latency_ms, generation_p999_latency_ms, request_queue_time_ms (per model and per route). Sudden step increases in p99 that persist > 2 minutes are the primary alert trigger.
- Throughput signals: tokens_out_per_minute (per pool), model_invocations_per_minute. Throughput drop correlated with latency increase indicates backpressure rather than pure demand surge.
- Resource signals: GPU_utilization_pct (per GPU), GPU_power_watts, GPU_temp_celsius, GPU_memory_used_mb. Watch for uneven distribution across cards on the same node (one card 90%+ while others 10–20%).
- Scheduler signals: pods_restarts_count, pod_evictions, node_allocatable_gpus, node_pods_count. A sudden cluster-wide uptick in pod_scheduling_latency is especially suspicious.
- Cache signals: kv_cache_hit_rate, kv_cache_evictions_per_min. High eviction rate plus low hit-rate implies prefix fragmentation; workloads may be thrashing KV caches across nodes.
- Batch/queueing signals: average_batch_size_tokens, batch_wait_time_ms. If batch sizes collapse while latency rises, suspect aggressive admission throttling or cache-miss amplification.

Quick triage checklist (first 10 minutes):
1) Confirm scope: identify affected pool(s) and customer(s) via route -> pool mapping.
   - Query: group by pool: sum(tokens_out_per_minute) and p99 latency.
2) Spike/latency correlation: are p99 spikes across all nodes in the pool or just a subset?
   - If subset: proceed to noisy-neighbor isolation.
   - If all nodes: consider autoscaler/queueing misconfig or external traffic surge.
3) Check GPU-level health on suspicious nodes:
   - Run: kubectl -n serving get pods -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node>
   - Run: ssh node && nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,utilization.gpu,utilization.memory,temperature.gpu,power.draw,memory.used --format=csv
   - Look for cards with very different utilization or cards reporting high temperature/power throttling.
4) KV cache health:
   - Check kv_cache_hit_rate and kv_cache_evictions_per_min for model variants pinned to the pool.
   - If eviction spikes align with latency, consider temporarily disabling cross-node placement (soft affinity) to boost local cache hit-rate.
5) Autoscaler signals:
   - Inspect autoscaler decisions in the last 15–30 minutes: scale_up_requests, scale_down_count, cooldown_remaining_seconds.
   - Look for repeated small scale-up -> immediate scale-down cycles (oscillation). Could be cooldown misconfig or wrong metric window.
6) Apply quick mitigations (see next section).

Immediate mitigation recipes (ordered by risk):
- Low risk, fast: enable model-variant fallback route for affected customer(s) to a compatible smaller/quantized variant (route-level override). This reduces per-request GPU memory pressure and increases effective throughput.
- Medium risk: cordon and drain suspect node(s) one at a time (kubectl cordon; drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=30). Monitor whether latency recovers while draining.
- Medium risk: disable autoscaler scale-down for 10–30 minutes to avoid oscillation while we stabilize load.
- Higher risk: relocate KV cache shards (if using local cache) by restarting lightweight cache-manager with sticky affinity to warm a new node; only if safe and with traffic-control.

Detailed diagnostic commands and quick PromQL snippets:
- Per-pool p99: sum by (pool) (histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(generation_latency_bucket[2m])) by (le, pool)))
- KV cache eviction rate: sum by (pool, model) (rate(kv_cache_evictions_total[1m]))
- GPU util split per node: avg by (node, gpu_index) (rate(gpu_utilization_percent[1m]))
- Pods per node: count by (node) (kube_pod_info{namespace=\"serving\"})
- Autoscaler cooldown remaining: max by (pool) (autoscaler_cooldown_seconds_remaining)
- Example kubectl for busy pods: kubectl -n serving top pod --containers | sort -k3 -n -r | head -n 20

Noisy neighbor isolation playbook (more granular):
1) Identify top resource consumers (per-node): top 5 pods by GPU memory usage and GPU util.
2) Map those pods to customers/routes. If a single tenant owns > 50% of GPU time on a node, label it noisy-candidate.
3) Apply ephemeral QoS throttle: set limit on max_batch_tokens or concurrency for that route (route-level throttle config) to damp the noisy tenant and buy time.
4) If throttling not effective, progressively migrate the noisy pods using migration policy: schedule to alternative nodes that currently have low GPU mem pressure (prefer nodes with cached prefixes for same model variant).
5) After migration, monitor kv_cache_hit_rate: moving a hot tenant may cause cache warmup blips. Consider pre-warming or allowing cache-warmup traffic via controlled traffic shift.

Autoscaler misconfig signatures and fixes:
Symptoms: repeated small scale-ups during burst then scale-downs in <cooldown window, pool-wide instability, or slow reaction causing backlog.
Potential causes and fixes:
- Cause: cooldown window shorter than time-to-warm (KV cache warming + model load). Fix: increase scale-up stabilization window to at least 3x median model load time (empirically 180–600s for large models).
- Cause: metric used for autoscale is instantaneous GPU util rather than sustained token-based metric. Fix: switch scale metric to tokens_per_gpu_minute with a moving-average window (2–5m).
- Cause: scheduler preemption/probing mislabels node capacity (labels mismatch after node upgrade). Fix: audit node labels for allocatable gpu counts and restart node agent on nodes flagged.

Unusual failure modes we saw (notes from investigations):
- KV-cache fragmentation: aggressive bin-packing placed many small tenants across nodes, creating many cold cache shards; when burst arrived, cache misses amplified host-to-host network reads and throttled batch formation.
- Thermal/driver-induced throttling: one model of GPU firmware we upgraded in 2024 had an edge-case with fan-profile changes leading to transient throttling under rapid power swings. This manifested as one card hitting 85–90C while sibling card idle.
- Batch collapse effect: admission controller dropped batch-size target when queue latency exceeded threshold, which reduced batch efficiency and increased per-token overhead; this happened during scale-down oscillations.

Post-incident follow-ups and long-term fixes (owners + rough ETA):
- Audit and adjust autoscaler metric and cooldown windows (owner: Miles Chen, ETA: 2 weeks).
- Add an explicit KV-cache warmup policy on pod start that pins a small warmup traffic slice for 90–180s (owner: Sofia Rodriguez, ETA: 3 weeks).
- Node-firmware rollback plan for affected GPU model with thermal profile (owner: Liam O'Connor + infra-hardware, ETA: 1 week to validate).
- Implement 'noisy-tenant score' per node and auto-throttle top scorer (owner: eng-sre, tracker: JIRA-NTS-27, ETA: 4 weeks).
- Improve observability: add per-card thermal anomaly alerts and cross-card-utilization-imbalance metric (owner: observability, ETA: 2 weeks).

Playbook for postmortem synthesis (if incident escalates to SEV):
1) secure timeline of all schedule/scale events and PVC/ephemeral-storage ops for the pool.
2) capture snapshots of nvidia-smi outputs for suspect nodes.
3) record exact route -> model_variant mappings and any runtime overrides (throttles/fallbacks).
4) reconstruct KV-cache metrics around the window with 10s resolution if available.
5) correlate with any infra changes (deploys, node reboots, driver rollouts) in the 24 hours preceding incident.

Open questions we still need to answer (hypotheses to validate):
- How much of the observed throughput loss is explained by cache cold-start vs thermal throttling? (Action: synthetic replay traffic that reproduces prefix diversity; measure hit-rate and per-node latency.)
- Does the autoscaler react to transient spikes because the metric window is too small? (Action: run controlled load test while toggling autoscaler window.)
- Is there an admission-control bug that reduces batch size incorrectly under certain queue latency shapes? (Action: add instrumentation to log batch_size decisions and upstream queue_length at decision point.)

Quick reference (cheat-sheet commands):
- List pods on node: kubectl -n serving get pods -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node>
- Drain node quickly: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=30 --timeout=5m
- Cordon node: kubectl cordon <node>
- Top pods by GPU mem (namespace serving): kubectl -n serving top pod --containers | sort -k3 -n -r | head -n 20
- Remote GPU info: ssh ops@<node> sudo nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,utilization.gpu,utilization.memory,temperature.gpu,power.draw,memory.used --format=csv

Notes on communication and runbook discipline:
- For customer-impacting incidents, label the incident channel with affected-pool and suspected-cause to make paging and escalation clearer (e.g., #inc-4532:pool-east1-noisy-kv).
- Keep mitigations reversible and small; prioritize steps that avoid data loss.
- Where we apply route-level fallbacks, capture the exact override and time so Product/Support can rollback if it changes quality unexpectedly.

Appendix: quick timeline example from a prior event (anonymized):
- 09:07 UTC: external traffic spike to customer X begins. p99 begins to creep up.
- 09:09 UTC: p99 crosses alert threshold for pool-east1 (inc-4532 page).
- 09:12 UTC: investigation shows 3 nodes with card-0 at 92C while card-1/2/3 low util. KV_cache_evictions spike.
- 09:18 UTC: cordon + drain node-17, enable variant-fallback for customer X. p99 falls toward baseline over 5 minutes.
- 09:40 UTC: autoscaler observed oscillation; scale-down disabled for 20 minutes.
- 10:05 UTC: nodes rebooted for driver rollback (after infra signoff).

Last updated notes:
- This is a living doc. If you add an experiment result, append a short entry with date, experiment description, and outcome so we can converge on root cause quickly.
- If you make a permanent config change based on this doc, add the PR link to 'linked_artifacts'.

TODO (short list):

End of document.
